verdicts.note: The Summary narrows whom the consequences fall on. The statement speaks of the effects of use in general and adds three wider kinds of consequence without saying for whom. The Summary makes the effects what use "does to a person" and the three wider kinds what use means for "the person's dealings" with other people, the law and money, so only the user's own consequences remain; what use costs a family or other people, which the statement's general terms cover, is left out. Fix: give the effects and the three kinds of consequence without tying them to the user. Limits is in order. Not a near copy. Wording and code equal the PDF (page 38, printed as 1.1.A under Standard 1 of the grade's pages); the statement starts and ends where the record does.

Round 2. The round 1 fault is resolved: the Summary no longer ties the effects, or the three wider kinds of consequence, to the user; it says what comes of use and what use means among people, before the law and in money. All four groups of substances and both time spans are kept. Not a near copy. Remark, not a fault: Limits calls the three wider kinds "beyond health"; the statement has no word for health, and the phrase sets no limit. Wording and code equal the PDF, read on the page image (page 38, printed without the grade under Standard 1 of the grade's pages); the statement starts and ends where the record does.

"In a child's hands" adds clinical claims the statement does not contain. Its last sentence has the child say how sadness after a loss differs from "depression that lasts": the statement asks for three things about each of the three matters it names; it does not ask the child to tell two of them apart, and it gives no criterion, such as how long it lasts, for the third. The bracketed list of what can bring them on also ends in "no clear cause", a claim about the third matter that the statement does not make. Take the differentiating sentence out, or keep the activity to what the statement asks for each of the three (how it shows, what brings it on, what it does to health). Smaller: Limits calls all three "conditions"; the second is an event in a life, not a condition. Wording and code match the PDF (page 40, printed as 1.1.M under Standard 1; the statement starts and ends where the record does). The Summary is faithful and is not a near copy.

Round 2. The round 1 fault is resolved: the sentence that had the child tell sadness after a loss from lasting depression is gone, and so is "no clear cause"; Limits now says three subjects. Looked through the whole record for clinical claims, durations and warning signs: no duration and no criterion remains. What remains is examples of the things the statement asks for (signs and causes in brackets, pooled over the three subjects) and, in Common mistakes, two points of the pack's own: that children use "depressed" for any sad day, and that stress shows in the body. Both stand under the pack's-inference heading and contradict nothing; reported to the lead. The Summary is faithful and not a near copy. Limits is right about 6.5.2.M. Wording and code equal the PDF, read on the page image (page 40, printed without the grade under Standard 1 of the grade's pages); the statement starts and ends where the record does.

All three problems are kept, and Limits is right that settling a disagreement in practice is 6.7.1.S. Not a near copy. Two things in the Summary. (1) It narrows whom the risks fall on to the "person who joins a gang or spends time with one". The statement speaks of the risks in general, and the record's own notes count the danger to the family among them. (2) It says what the involvement is (joining, or spending time with a gang). The statement uses one general word for it and, as the record's own Limits says, does not say what counts. Fix: say what risks being involved with a gang brings, without naming forms of involvement or whose risks they are. Not a near copy. Wording and code equal the PDF (page 37, printed as 1.3.S under Standard 1 of the grade's pages); the statement starts and ends where the record does.

"In a child's hands" names particular conditions (diabetes, asthma, a wheelchair, a blood-sugar check). They are examples inside the two general terms the statement itself uses, so confirmed; the statement names none of them.

Limits, last sentence: it reports the footnote only in part. On the page (37) the statement carries a raised 1, and the footnote at the foot of the page points to two places, one section of the Education Code and the document's own glossary, and says what for: what the statement's key noun means in law. Limits says only that a footnote cites the Education Code, next to a sentence that the statement lists no kind of weapon. Nothing is contradicted (the glossary entry, PDF page 71, is a general definition with one exclusion and no list of kinds), but a designer is not told that a legal definition exists and where it is. Fix: say that the footnote points both to the Education Code and to the glossary, where a weapon is defined in law. The same Limits sentence was left as a note in the kindergarten, grade 1 and grade 4 checks; it is the reason here because this check was asked to hold Limits to reporting the footnote in full. Wording: the record leaves the raised digit out and does not end in a bracketed digit, which is form; the footnote equals the record's accompanying text apart from the export's bracketed marker. Summary faithful, all three settings kept. Not a near copy. Wording and code equal the PDF (page 37, printed as 1.5.S under Standard 1 of the grade's pages); the statement starts and ends where the record does.

Two things. (1) The Summary adds an owner: "when they are stressed, grieving a loss, or depressed" makes the trouble the help-seeker's own. The statement does not say whose it is, so seeking help because of a friend's or a relative's trouble is covered too; the record's own "In a child's hands" includes such a case (a friend who says they want to disappear). Write it without tying the three to the person who seeks help. (2) "In a child's hands" adds clinical thresholds the statement does not contain: the cases carry fixed durations (two weeks, a month) and the child is to give the deciding sign as how long it lasts, how strong it is, whether daily things can still be done, and any talk of self-harm. The statement gives no situations and no warning signs, as the record's own Limits says; the sorting into "handle it" and "get help" by these criteria is the pack's, and a designer could take it for the standard's. Mark the cases as examples without fixed durations, or drop the criteria. Wording and code match the PDF (page 41, printed as 5.2.M under Standard 5; the statement starts and ends where the record does). Not a near copy; the cross-reference to 6.1.1.M in Limits is right.

(2) "In a child's hands" no longer sorts cases by criteria: the durations and the deciding signs are gone, three short cases are marked as the pack's examples, and no case is assigned to the side of needing help. Looked through the whole record for clinical claims, durations and warning signs: none in the Summary, in "In a child's hands" or in Limits. One remains in Common mistakes: a friend's talk of harming themselves that is kept secret. It stands under the pack's-inference heading, sets no criterion and contradicts nothing, so it is not counted; reported to the lead, who asked that nothing of the kind remain. Wording and code equal the PDF, read on the page image (page 41, printed without the grade under Standard 5 of the grade's pages); the statement starts and ends where the record does.

Summary faithful (no owner of the three troubles; the circumstances in which a person ought to look for help) and not a near copy.
